newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity seen opening up with cash, heat.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity seen opening up with cash, heat.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures were called to open higher Tuesday, extending yesterday's gain on surging physical power prices in the western U.S. due to strong air-conditioning demand.
"It's the heat in southern California, and there's a lot of humidity too," a Houston futures trader said, referring to the reasons behind surging futures and cash prices.

In over-the-counter activity, September Palo Verde (PV) futures were quoted at $32.60-32.80 a megawatt hour (MWh) up from Monday's $31.04, while September California-Oregon Border (COB) was talked at $24.75-25.25 up from $24.35 yesterday.
September PV seemed poised to surpass its life-of-contract high at $31.60.
In early cash business, next-day firm, peak prices at PV leaped $15.00-25.00 to $55.00-65.00 a MWh, while those at COB jumped more than five dollars to $29.00-30.00.

Much of the western U.S. were predicted to feel sweltering heat through Thursday with the exception of Wyoming, Colorado and New Mexico which were expected to experience much cooler than normal conditions.
In the six to 10 day forecasts, temperatures in the Southwest would cool toward more seasonal levels, while those in the Northwest would stay near to slightly above normal.
Electricity output from the 1,221 megawatt (MW) Palo Verde nuclear power unit 3 in Wintersburg, Ariz., held at 90 percent power early Tuesday for repairs to a condensate pump.
The unit was expected to return to full power within the next 48 hours, a spokesman for the plant said.
The adjacent 1,221 MW Palo Verde nuclear power unit 2 was operating at 93 percent of capacity as of early Monday as the unit coasts down to a scheduled refueling outage September 6.
Water flow into regional hydroelectric systems in the Northwest and Canada has been slowed in recent days to refill reservoirs for fish migration requirements.
Many cash traders wanted to complete their power schedules for the rest of the week ahead of a two-day meeting called by the Western Systems Power Pool, traders said.

Transmission capacity on the Pacific Intertie, which links the Pacific Northwest to Southern Califoria, was tentatively set to increase to 6,900 MW from 6,300 MW midnight Monday pending final approval of system operating procedures.
